name: PEG filler

lead:
PEG filler refers to injectable products that use polyethylene glycol, a synthetic polymer, as the volumising material. It is one of several synthetic filler types listed in the medical literature, alongside poly(lactic acid), polyacrylamide and others, and sits beside the far more common hyaluronic acid fillers.
The appearance goal is the same as for other fillers: restoring or adding volume to hollows, lines or facial contours. Public information on PEG-based fillers specifically is thin, and polyethylene glycol is far better known in other medical roles, such as laxatives, eye drops and drug conjugation.

paras: Fillers in general are placed by a trained clinician with injections into targeted areas of the face, and some are built as crosslinked hydrogels that hold water and keep their shape. Specific techniques, products and volumes are a matter for medical practitioners and are not covered here.

Dermal fillers as a class can cause bruising, redness, pain and itching, less often infection or allergic lumps, and rarely vascular embolisation that can lead to permanent blindness or skin necrosis. Risks differ by product and injector, and regulators and clinicians should be consulted for any particular filler.

chain: Injectable polymer placed in the tissue
angle.text: Fillers add volume at the injection site, which can soften lines or reshape contours. PEG is one of the synthetic filler materials, used less commonly than hyaluronic acid.

lead: Polyethylene glycol (PEG) is a synthetic polymer with many medical uses. In aesthetics, it is named among the synthetic materials used in injectable dermal fillers, next to poly(lactic acid), poly(methyl methacrylate), polyacrylamide and dextran, while hyaluronic acid is the most common filler overall [1].

Some fillers are hydrogels: networks of water-retaining polymers, physically or chemically crosslinked, with chemical crosslinking generally giving greater stability [1]. Looksmaxxing discussion places PEG-based filler under hardmaxxing, the group of surgical and injectable methods for changing facial structure.
Published studies of PEG in the biomedical literature mostly concern its use as a laxative, in artificial tears and in PEGylated drugs rather than as a facial filler [2][3].

paras: PEG is listed with other synthetic polymers used in filler products, and hydrogel fillers rely on crosslinked polymer networks that retain water [1].

Dermal fillers in general can cause bruising, redness, pain and itching; less commonly infection or allergic reactions leading to scarring or lumps; and rarely vascular embolisation that can cause permanent blindness or delayed skin necrosis [1]. These are class-wide figures and not specific to PEG products.

No studies have tested PEG as a facial dermal filler. Studies of polyethylene glycol exist for other uses, including artificial tears, constipation and PEGylated drugs, and are not about appearance [2][3].
